### Immunoaffinity purification and immunoblotting of FICD

The absence of FICD protein in AR42j FICD-/- cells was confirmed by immunoaffinity purification as the endogenous protein could not be detected by immunoblotting of total lysates. Protein extracts from wildtype and FICD-/- AR42j cells were prepared in HG lysis buffer containing protease inhibitors, cleared, normalized and equal volumes of the lysates (4 mg total protein) were incubated with 15 µl UltraLink Hydrazine Resin (Pierce cat. # 53149, UK) on which FICD-specific chicken IgY antibodies have been covalently immobilized according to the manufacturer’s instructions (chicken anti-FICD) or rabbit polyclonal IgG antibodies against human FICD (rabbit anti-FICD; LifeSpan BioSciences) bound to Protein A Sepharose 4B beads (Invitrogen cat. #10-1041), for 16 hr at 4°C. The beads were then recovered by centrifugation for 1 min at 1,000 g and washed three times with HG lysis buffer. Bound proteins were eluted in 40 µl 2 x SDS sample buffer for 10 min at 70°C and equal volumes of the samples were loaded on a 12% SDS polyacrylamide gel, and endogenous FICD was detected by immunoblotting with rabbit anti-FICD or chicken anti-FICD antibodies. Samples of the normalized lysates (25 µg) were loaded and BiP was detected as an “input” control.

### In vitro AMPylation assay

Unless indicated otherwise, in vitro AMPylation was performed in AMPylation buffer (described above) by incubation of purified wildtype or mutant BiP proteins at 20 µM with bacterially expressed GST-FICDE234G (or as a control with inactive GST-FICDE234G-H363A) at 0.8 µM in presence of 1.5 mM ATP for 45 min at 30°C. The final volume of a typical reaction was 15 µl. The samples were then treated with or without the BiP linker-specific protease SubA at 30 ng/µl for 10 min at room temperature. Volumes corresponding to 7 µg BiP protein were loaded per lane on native or SDS polyacrylamide gels and visualized by Coomassie staining. The in vitro AMPylation time-course experiments presented in Figure 7C and D were performed likewise but after incubation for the indicated times at 30°C the reactions were stopped on ice by addition of 40 mM EDTA and samples were run immediately on native gels.

Radioactive in vitro AMPylation was performed by mixing 7.5 µg of purified wildtype or mutant BiP proteins with 10 µM non-radiolabeled ATP and 0.185 MBq α-32P-ATP (EasyTide; Perkin Elmer, UK) in a total volume of 30 µl in AMPylation buffer. The reactions were incubated with 5 µl GSH-Sepharose beads coupled with mammalian expressed GST-FICDE234G (or GST only) in 1.5 ml reaction tubes at 30°C on a thermomixer (Eppendorf) while shaking at 800 rpm. After 45 min [in these experiments a time before the reaction went to completion to reveal differences in AMPylation amongst BiP mutants (Figure 5A and C and Figure 7A)] the beads were sedimented by centrifugation and the reaction was terminated by addition of SDS loading buffer to the supernatants and heating for 5 min at 75°C. Equal volumes of the samples were loaded on 12% SDS polyacrylamide gels. Proteins were visualized by Coomassie staining and radioactive signals were detected with a Typhoon Trio imager (GE Healthcare) upon overnight exposure of the dried gels to a storage phosphor screen. To test the sensitivity of AMPylated BiP towards cleavage by SubA ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1), 6 µg of purified BiPT229A were labeled in 60 µl AMPylation buffer containing 6.7 MBq of α-32P-ATP and 10 µl of GST-FICDE234G-coupled beads as described above. After incubation for 30 min at 30°C non-radioactive ATP was added at 5 µM and the reaction was allowed to proceed for another 60 min. The beads were then sedimented by centrifugation and 1.5 mM ATP was added to the supernatant. To remove nucleotides the sample was passed through a Sephadex G-50 MicroSpin column (illustra AutoSeq G-50; GE Healthcare) equilibrated with AMPylation buffer. 1.5 µg of the recovered protein was mixed with 60 µg unmodified BiPT229A (at 0.6 mg/ml final) in presence of 1.5 mM ATP and the combined sample was divided into fractions to which SubA (from a dilution series) was added to yield final concentrations between 0.08 and 120 ng/µl. After incubation for 30 min at room temperature the proteins were denatured with SDS sample buffer and equal volumes were applied to SDS-PAGE, Coomassie-stained and signals were detected by autoradiography.

### Purification of in vitro AMPylated BiP proteins

Twenty mg of purified wiltype BiP or BiPV461F protein were in vitro AMPylated for 2 hr at 30°C with 1 mg bacterially expressed GST-FICDE234G in presence of 1.5 mM ATP in AMPylation buffer in a final volume of 12 ml. BiP proteins were then bound to 400 µl nickel affinity matrix, washed with AMPylation buffer and eluted in AMPylation buffer containing 250 mM imidazole. The concentrated eluate was divided into aliquots and immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C. For applications that required complete absence of detergent or imidazole the affinity chromatography eluate was passed through a Centri•Pure P25 desalting column (emp BIOTECH, Germany) equilibrated in HKM buffer followed by concentration of the proteins using centrifugal filters (Amicon Ultra, 30 kDa MWCO; Merck Millipore) before freezing. The in vitro modified proteins were used for mass spectrometry analyses and functional assays (see below). Unmodified BiP from parallel mock in vitro AMPylation reactions, to which no enzyme has been added, served as controls in all assays.

### Preparation of SILAC samples

The experimental strategy for the stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) experiment is outlined in Figure 6A and samples were prepared as follows: Wildtype and FICD-/- CHO-K1 cells were adapted to Ham’s F12 medium minus L-arginine and L-lysine for SILAC (Pierce cat. # 88424) supplemented with 10% (v/v) dialyzed fetal bovine serum (Gibco; Life Technologies cat. # 26400-044), 1 x Penicillin-Streptomycin (Sigma), 2 mM L-glutamine (Sigma), 280 mg/l L-proline (Sigma cat. # P5607-25G), 62.5 mg/l “light” L-lysine monohydrochloride (Sigma cat. # L8662-25G) and 60.5 mg/l “light” L-arginine monohydrochloride (Sigma cat. # A6969-25G) and incubated as described above. Once adapted, the cells were cultured in SILAC medium containing either 60.5 mg/l “light” (as above) or “heavy” L-arginine monohydrochloride (R10; U-13C6, U-15N4; Cambridge Isotope Laboratories, Inc. cat. # CNLM-539, Andover, MO) for several passages (> 15 cell divisions) before expansion in five 10 cm dishes per sample. The cells were grown to ~70% confluence and medium was exchanged 14 hr before treatment with or without 100 µg/ml cycloheximide for 3 hr. After washing with ice-cold PBS the cells were collected in PBS containing 1 mM EDTA and lysed in Triton lysis buffer [20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 10% (v/v) glycerol] containing protease inhibitors. The protein concentrations of the cleared lysates were normalized and equal volumes were then mixed (1:1 ratio) as indicated. Each combined sample was pre-cleared for 15 min at 4°C with 30 µl blocked UltraLink Hydrazine Resin followed by immunoaffinity purification for 2 hr at 4°C with 30 µl of the same resin to which BiP-specific IgY antibodies were covalently coupled (Preissler et al., 2015). The beads were washed twice for 10 min with lysis buffer, once with lysis buffer containing 350 mM NaCl and once again with lysis buffer, before elution in 2x non-reducing SDS sample buffer for 10 min at 70°C. Afterwards, the beads were removed by centrifugation and the supernatants were supplemented with 125 mM DTT, heated for 5 min at 70°C and loaded on a 12% SDS polyacrylamide gel. The gel was stained with Coomassie and bands corresponding in size to BiP were cut out for in-gel digest with Arg-C endopeptidase, and analysis by mass spectrometry.

### Immunoaffinity purification of intact endogenous BiP for mass determination

Wildtype and FICD-/- CHO-K1 cells were grown in standard medium (ten 10 cm dishes per sample) and treated for 3 hr with 100 µg/ml cycloheximide before cell lysis with Triton lysis buffer supplemented with protease inhibitors and BiP was immunoaffinity purified as described above with the following modifications: The lysates (~4 mg protein per sample) were pre-cleared with 40 µl blocked UltraLink Hydrazine Resin for 30 min at 4°C followed by incubation for 2 hr with 60 µl of the resin carrying covalently attached BiP-specific IgY antibodies. The beads were washed sequentially for 10 min with lysis buffer, lysis buffer containing 350 mM NaCl, HG buffer (see above) containing 1 mM ATP, and once again with lysis buffer. Bound protein was eluted in 150 µl of 0.2 M glycine-HCl pH 2.5 for 10 min at 16°C followed by neutralization of the recovered sample supernatants with 1/10 volume of 1.5 M Tris-HCl pH 8.8. Afterwards, protein was precipitated with isopropanol and analyzed by mass spectrometry.

### Mass spectrometry

Molecular masses of intact BiP proteins were measured by electrospray ionization mass spectrometry using a Q-Trap 4000 (ABSciex) after ‘on-line’ reverse-phase chromatographic purification of samples as described previously (Carroll et al., 2009). The instrument was operated in MS mode, and was calibrated with a mixture of myoglobin and trypsinogen. Reconstructed molecular masses were calculated with Bioanalyst (ABSciex) and masses from amino acid sequences with MassLynx (Waters).

To analyze masses of BiP peptides, proteins were reduced, alkylated and digested “in-gel”. In vitro AMPylated BiP protein was digested with the proteolytic enzymes as indicated and SILAC samples were digested using Arg-C. The resulting peptides were analyzed by LC-MS/MS using either an Orbitrap XL coupled to a nanoAcquity UHPLC or a Q Exactive coupled to a RSLC3000 UHPLC. Data was processed in Proteome Discoverer 1.4 using Sequest to search a UniProt E. coli database (downloaded 29/04/15, 4,378 entries) with the sequence for Chinese hamster (Cricetulus griseus) BiP added or a Chinese Hamster database (downloaded 19/02/14, 23,884 entries). Oxidation (M), deamidation (N/Q) and AMPylation (S/T) were set as variable modifications and carbamidomethylation (C) as a fixed modification. FDR calculations were performed by Percolator and peptides were filtered to 1%. Peak areas were determined using the Precursor Ion Quantifier node in Proteome Discoverer.

### Isoelectric focusing (IEF)

Purified untagged hamster BiP19-654 at 15 µM was in vitro AMPylated with 0.75 µM GST-FICDE234G (or as a control with inactive GST-FICDE234G-H363A) in presence of 1.5 mM ATP for the indicated times at 30°C as described above. The reactions were then treated without or with 30 ng/µl SubA for 10 min at room temperature in a final volume of 20 µl and analyzed by IEF as described previously (Chambers et al., 2012; Laitusis et al., 1999) with modifications: The samples were diluted with 180 µl of IEF sample buffer [8 M urea, 5% (w/v) CHAPS, 50 mM DTT, 2% (v/v) Pharmalyte (pH 4.5-5.4; GE Healthcare)] and loaded on a 3.75% polyacrylamide gel containing 8.8 M urea, 1.25% (w/v) CHAPS and 5% (v/v) Pharmalyte. The loaded samples were overlaid with 0.5 M urea and 2% (v/v) Pharmalyte solution before separation. 10 mM glutamic acid and 50 mM histidine were used as anode and cathode buffers, respectively. After the run (100V, 10 min; 250V, 1 hr; 300V, 1 hr; 500V, 30 min) proteins were transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane in blotting buffer [25 mM Tris-HCl pH 9.2, 190 mM glycine, 0.01% (w/v) SDS, 10% (v/v) methanol] for 3 hr at 300 mA and immunodetected with BiP-specific antibodies as described above.

Lysate samples from mammalian cells (CHO-K1 and AR42j) were prepared for analysis by IEF as follows: Cells were grown in 10 cm dishes to approximately 90% confluence, washed with ice-cold TBS, resuspended in 1 ml TBS, sedimented by centrifugation, and lysed in 30 x its packed cell volume of IEF lysis buffer [8.8 M urea, 5% (w/v) CHAPS, 1 µM sodium pyrophosphate, 2 mM imidodiphosphate, 50 mM DTT and 2% (v/v) Pharmalyte] at room temperature for 5 min. The lysates were then centrifuged at 20,238 g for 10 min at room temperature, the supernatants were transferred to a new tube and then centrifuged again for 60 min. The cleared lysates (50 µl) were then purified using Sephadex G-50 MicroSpin columns equilibrated with IEF sample buffer, diluted 1:2 in IEF sample buffer and 15 µl were loaded on a 3.75% polyacrylamide gel followed by BiP immunoblotting as described above.

### Malachite green ATPase assay

Malachite green (MG) reaction solution was prepared freshly by mixing stock solutions of MG dye [0.111% (w/v) malachite green, 6 N sulphuric acid], 7.5% (w/v) ammonium molybdate and 11% (v/v) Tween 20 in a 10:2.5:0.2 ratio. Samples of purified BiP proteins (5 µM) were incubated in HKM with 3 mM ATP in a final volume of 20 µl for 60 min at 30°C. 15 µl of each sample were then diluted with 135 µl water on a 96-well plate, mixed with 50 µl MG reaction solution and incubated for 2 min at room temperature. 20 µl of a 34% (w/v) sodium citrate solution were added to quench the reactions and after incubation for further 30 min the absorbance was measured at 612 nm with a plate reader (Infinite F500; Tecan). Standard curves were prepared with serial dilutions of KH2PO4 and served as a reference to calculate Vmax values. Statistical analysis by unpaired t-test was performed using Graphpad Prism version 6.

### Fluorescence polarization (FP) measurements

Binding of substrate peptide by purified BiP proteins was measured as previously described (Chambers et al., 2012; Marcinowski et al., 2011) with modifications: Unmodified or in vitro AMPylated BiP proteins were incubated at the indicated concentrations (between 0 and 40 µM) with 1 µM lucifer yellow (LY)-labeled substrate peptide (HTFPAVLGSC) in presence of 1 mM ADP for 24 hr at 30°C in FP buffer [37.5 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.4, 125 mM KCl, 7 mM MgCl2, 0.5 mM CaCl2, 125 mM imidazole, 0.05% (v/v) Triton X-100]. 20 µl of each sample were transferred to a 386-well polystyrene microplate (µClear, black; greiner bio-one cat. # 781096, UK) and fluorescence polarization of the lucifer yellow fluorophore was measured (excitation λ = 430 nm; emission λ = 535 nm) at room temperature in a plate reader. For analysis of competitive substrate dissociation, BiP proteins (40 µM) were incubated with LY-labeled substrate peptide (1 µM) as described above. Afterwards, 400-fold molar excess of unlabeled substrate peptide (HTFPAVL) was added to the pre-formed BiP:substrate complexes and the change in fluorescence polarization was measured over time. From each value the background signal of a reference sample containing only LY-labeled peptide (without BiP protein) were subtracted.

### Reverse transcription of cellular mRNA and quantitative PCR

RNA from CHO-K1 cells was extracted using RNA Stat-60 (Amsbio, UK) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. 1 µg RNA was reverse transcribed with Oligo(dT)18 primer using RevertAid Reverse Transcriptase (Thermo Scientific, UK). Quantitative PCR analysis was performed using the Power SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) according to the manufacturer’s instructions on a 7900HT Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems). FICD, RPL27 (60S ribosomal protein L27) and PPIA (cyclophilin A) were amplified using the following primers: FICD-F 5’-GGGCTGCTGACTGTTAAGACTA-3’, FICD-R 5’-CCTTGACGCTTCATCTCCA-3’, RPL27-F 5’-ACAATCACCTCATGCCCACAAG-3’, RPL27-R 5’-GCGTTTCAGGGCTGGGTCTC-3’, PPIA-F 5’-TTCCTCCTTTCACAGAATTATCCC-3’, and PPIA-R 5’-CTGCCGCCAGTGCCATTATG-3’. Relative quantities of amplified cDNAs were then determined using SDS 2.4.1 software (Applied Biosystems) and normalized to PPIA mRNA.

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "AMPylation matches BiP activity to client protein load to prevent over-chaperoning of the endoplasmic reticulum" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Randy Schekman (Senior Editor) and three reviewers, one of whom, Reid Gilmore, is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The manuscript from Preissler et al. investigates AMPylation of BiP. BiP was known to undergo a modification in the ER, which was believed to be ADP-ribosylation based upon incorporation of phosphate and adenosine. Previously, the Ron lab indirectly mapped the sites of ADP-ribosylation to two arginines in the substrate-binding domain (SBD) of BiP. Two recent papers established that the modification is AMPylation, not ADP-ribosylation, and identified an ER localized enzyme (FICD/HYPE) that is likely responsible for the modification. However, contradictory conclusions were reached concerning the location of the AMPylated residue (ATPase domain or SBD) and the impact of AMPylation on BiP activity and UPR signaling. In the current manuscript, Preissler et al. use a combination of in vitro AMPylation experiments and cell culture experiments to convincingly demonstrate the following: (a) FICD modifies a single site in the substrate binding domain of BiP both in vitro and in cells, (b) the primary modification site is T518, (c) AMPylation of BiP reduces BiPs ATPase rate and renders it less-responsive to J domain containing proteins, (d) excessive AMPylation of BiP is toxic to cells due to constitutive activation of the UPR and (e) a block in AMPylation of BiP blunts the early response of cells to ER stress. One weakness of the paper is that the effects of constitutive AMPylation or inhibited AMPylation on UPR signaling are relatively small. It thus remains unclear whether the modification has an important physiological role. The subtle change in the kinetics of UPR activation that was observed in the FIDC null cells is probably not sufficient to warrant the title of the manuscript. This is a solid and interesting paper that should be appropriate for publication in eLife after modifications to address the major points listed below.

Essential revisions:

1) The manuscript should include a serious discussion of the previous data reported by the Ron group and other labs to clarify whether a modification at T518 can account for the previous findings. For example, is the weaker effect of point mutations (R470E and R492E) on in vitro AMPylation in the current manuscript explained by differences in assay conditions? The Ham and Orth groups reported AMPylation in the NBD, yet reached conflicting conclusions on the effect of this modification on ATP hydrolysis by BiP. The authors should comment on how a modification of a threonine residue in a loop linking the SBD and how NBD could affect ATP hydrolysis.

2) The other two groups reported that FicD/HYPE is up-regulated by ER stress. Have the authors of the current manuscript determined whether HYPE is induced by the UPR? If so, are the kinetics of up-regulation slow enough to suggest that UPR induced HYPE expression is a mechanism to inactivate the excess BiP made during a stress response? If not how does this fit their hypothesis?

3) A central conclusion of the current manuscript is that modification of a single site (T518) can account for all previous evidence that BiP was modified by adenosine and phosphate. The BiP and AMPylated BiP that were used for electrospray mass spectroscopy eluted as broad, tailing peaks on the LC column (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Prominent shoulders (71.3 min and 73.7 min) were present in both the BiP and BiP-AMP samples. Were the tailing sections of the BiP and BiP-AMP peak analyzed by ES-MS, and do they contain BiP with different, or additional modifications?

4) Why is the FL/BiP ratio high (7.18, 7.48) in cells that have the constitutively active FICD plasmid in the absence of doxycycline (Figure 9C)? Are low levels of FICD expressed in the absence of DOX? Faint bands in -Dox lanes also seem to be present in control cells, which do not have a high FL/BiP ratio. The authors should comment on this discrepancy.

5) The kinetics of peptide dissociation from BiP-AMP looks very biphasic even when the time scale is 0-60 min. The data should also be fit assuming a biphasic dissociation rate. If such a fit is superior, this raises the question of whether the BiP-AMP sample is homogeneous. Could it contain some unmodified BiP? Or could it contain BiP AMPylated at a different site (T525 or T527)? The figure could be improved by having a dashed line showing the fluorescence polarization of free peptide expressed relative to the BiP-peptide and BiP-AMP peptide complexes. Figure 8E is the best evidence that AMPylation of BiP has an effect on the behavior of the chaperone in vitro, so the data need to be convincing. Please provide error bars.

6) The authors present evidence that the ATPase activity of BiP-AMP is not stimulated by the J-domain of ERdJ6. Failure of a J domain to stimulate hydrolysis of the modified protein is somewhat surprising, particularly since they have concluded that the ATP bound form of BiP is the substrate for AMPylation, which is also the preferred binding form for DnaJ proteins. Does the J domain still bind ATP BiP-AMP? Or do they suppose the AMPylation stimulate ATP hydrolysis rendering BiP resistant to J domain stimulation?

claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Covalent transformation(s) of BiP correlate inversely with the burden of unfolded proteins in the ER.
claims.source: These covalent transformation(s) of BiP correlate inversely with the burden of unfolded proteins in the ER (Chambers et al., 2012; Laitusis et al., 1999; Leno and Ledford, 1989)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The modified form of BiP was under-represented in complex with substrates.
claims.source: and because the modified form of BiP was under-represented in complex with substrates (Hendershot et al., 1988), were deemed to reflect inactivating modification(s) of the chaperone (Chambers et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Both 32P orthophosphate and 3H adenosine labeling mapped consistently to a cyanogen bromide (CnBr) cleavage fragment in the C-terminal substrate binding domain of BiP (Thr434 to Met541).
claims.source: A consensus emerged in regards to the region of BiP that bears the modification, as both 32P orthophosphate and 3H adenosine labeling mapped consistently to a cyanogen bromide (CnBr) cleavage fragment in the C-terminal substrate binding domain of BiP (Thr434 to Met541) (Chambers et al., 2012; Gaut, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Mutations in Arg470 and Arg492 markedly attenuated radiolabeling in vivo of FLAG-tagged BiP expressed in cells.
claims.source: Mutations in two arginine residues on that fragment (Arg470 and Arg492) markedly attenuated radiolabeling in vivo of FLAG-tagged BiP expressed in cells, suggesting that they might be the modification sites (Chambers et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: BiP is subject to AMPylation, which results in the formation of a phosphodiester bond between the alpha phosphate of ATP and a hydroxyl amino acid side chain.
claims.source: Recently it has been reported that BiP is subject to a different modification, AMPylation, which results in the formation of an phosphodiester bond between the alpha phosphate of ATP and a hydroxyl amino acid side chain (with release of pyrophosphate).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to recent work.

claims.claim: BiP AMPylation is effected by FICD (also known as HYPE).
claims.source: This modification of BiP is effected by a broadly conserved, ER-localized enzyme, FICD (also known as HYPE) (Ham et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citations to recent work.

claims.claim: The Orth lab provides evidence that AMPylation is an inactivation modification, induced when client protein burden is low.
claims.source: There is lack of unanimity in regards to the circumstances and consequences of BiP AMPylation: the Orth lab provides evidence that AMPylation is an inactivation modification, induced when client protein burden is low (Ham et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The Mattoo lab suggests that BiP AMPylation is an activating modification induced by ER stress.
claims.source: whereas the Mattoo lab suggests that it is an activating modification induced by ER stress (Sanyal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Inhibition of protein synthesis led to accumulation of a prominent high mobility species tentatively named 'B' form of BiP.
claims.source: Inhibition of protein synthesis led to accumulation of a prominent high mobility species tentatively named 'B' form
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Depletion of ER calcium progressively drew on the pool of 'B' form BiP to promote the assembly of BiP oligomers.
claims.source: whereas depletion of ER calcium progressively drew on this pool to promote the assembly of BiP oligomers (Preissler et al., 2015) (Figure 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claims.claim: The 'B' form of BiP was relatively resistant to cleavage in vitro by SubA protease.
claims.source: The 'B' form of BiP was also noted for its relative resistance to cleavage in vitro by a bacterial protease, SubA, which cuts BiP within a highly conserved linker sequence connecting the nucleotide binding domain (NBD) and substrate binding domain (SBD) (Paton et al., 2006) (Figure 1A and D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Resistance to cleavage by SubA is a feature of the acidic, modified form of BiP.
claims.source: Resistance to cleavage by SubA is also a feature of the acidic, modified form of BiP (Chambers et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The SubA-resistant 'B' form, prominent in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells, was conspicuously absent in FICD-/- cells.
claims.source: The SubA-resistant 'B' form, prominent in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells, was conspicuously absent in FICD-/- cells (compare lanes 2 and 5 in Figure 2B)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: FICD inactivation led to disappearance of the acidic form of BiP present in lysates of cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells resolved by isoelectric focusing PAGE.
claims.source: FICD inactivation also led to disappearance of the acidic form of BiP, present in lysates of cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells resolved by isoelectric focusing PAGE (IEF-PAGE, Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Mutation of glutamate 234 to glycine (FICDE234G) de-represses FICD.
claims.source: FICD-mediated AMPylation is strongly autoinhibited by intramolecular competition for ATP γ-phosphate binding by glutamate 234, whose mutation to glycine (FICDE234G) de-represses FICD
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Replacement of histidine 363 with alanine (FICDH363A) abolishes AMPylation activity.
claims.source: whereas replacement of histidine 363, which is located in the highly conserved catalytic FIC motif, with alanine (FICDH363A) abolishes AMPylation activity (Engel et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Enforced overexpression of the constitutively active FICDE234G led to the re-appearance of an acidic form of BiP in the FICD-/- cells.
claims.source: In keeping with these observations, enforced overexpression of the constitutively active FICDE234G led to the re-appearance of an acidic form of BiP in the FICD-/- cells (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Wildtype FICD did not promote BiP's acidic form, even when strongly overexpressed.
claims.source: Wildtype FICD did not promote BiP's acidic form, even when strongly overexpressed, suggesting the existence of robust inhibitory mechanisms restraining potentially deleterious effects of protein modification (Engel et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and citation to prior work.

claims.claim: A decline in 'B' form and an increase in susceptibility to digestion by SubA were noted within 2 hr of exposure of cells to 2-deoxyglucose.
claims.source: A decline in 'B' form and an increase in susceptibility to digestion by SubA were noted within 2 hr of exposure of cells to the reversible ER stress inducing agent 2-deoxyglucose ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Decline in 'B' form occurred in the face of a marked increase in FICD mRNA.
claims.source: This decline in 'B' form occurred in the face of a marked increase in FICD mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) (Ham et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Washout of 2-deoxyglucose was associated with progressive increase in 'B' form and the emergence of resistance to cleavage by SubA.
claims.source: Washout of 2-deoxyglucose was associated with progressive increase in 'B' form and the emergence of resistance to cleavage by SubA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and C.

claims.claim: Active FICDE234G promoted the ATP-dependent in vitro appearance of a 'B' form of recombinant BiP purified from bacteria.
claims.source: Whether purified as a GST-fusion protein from bacteria or from overexpressing mammalian cells, active FICDE234G promoted the ATP-dependent in vitro appearance of a 'B' form of recombinant BiP purified from bacteria.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The 'B' form constituted in vitro was partially resistant to cleavage by SubA.
claims.source: Like the endogenous 'B' form, found in cells, the 'B' form constituted in vitro was also partially resistant to cleavage by SubA (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Emergence of the 'B' form in vitro correlated with the acquisition of a faster migrating acidic form of BiP on IEF-PAGE.
claims.source: Emergence of the 'B' form in vitro correlated with the acquisition of a faster migrating acidic form of BiP on IEF-PAGE (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: FICD converted all the detectable BiP to a single acidic form in a time-dependent manner.
claims.source: FICD converted all the detectable BiP to a single acidic form in a time-dependent manner, which, like the endogenous acidic from of BiP, was also relatively resistant to cleavage by SubA (Figure 3B, lane 8).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Addition of purified active FICDE234G to lysates from FICD-/- cells entirely converted endogenous BiP into the acidic form.
claims.source: Likewise, addition of purified active FICDE234G to lysates from FICD-/- cells entirely converted endogenous BiP into the acidic form (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Within the resolution of IEF-PAGE, there is no evidence for heterogeneity in BiP modification.
claims.source: Of note, within the resolution of IEF-PAGE, there is no evidence for heterogeneity in BiP modification [also see (Carlsson and Lazarides, 1983; Laitusis et al., 1999)].
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: FICD efficiently transferred the 32P label from the alpha phosphate of ATP onto BiP, consistent with AMPylation.
claims.source: FICD efficiently transferred the 32P label from the alpha phosphate of ATP onto BiP, consistent with AMPylation (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Cleavage of radiolabeled BiP by SubA led to emergence of a radiolabeled substrate binding domain fragment (Leu417-Leu654).
claims.source: Interestingly, cleavage of radiolabeled BiP (by prolonged incubation with SubA) led to emergence of a radiolabeled substrate binding domain fragment (Leu417-Leu654); the nucleotide binding domain fragment, though conspicuous on the Coomassie-stained gel, was entirely devoid of label (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The nucleotide binding domain fragment of BiP cleaved by SubA was entirely devoid of radioactive label.
claims.source: the nucleotide binding domain fragment, though conspicuous on the Coomassie-stained gel, was entirely devoid of label (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The in vitro labeling pattern fits well with the metabolic labeling of BiP by 32P orthophosphate or 3H adenosine label donors in vivo.
claims.source: This in vitro labeling pattern fits well with the metabolic labeling of BiP by 32P orthophosphate or 3H adenosine label donors in vivo, as the label was mapped to a single CnBr cleavage fragment spanning Thr434 to Met541 (Chambers et al., 2012; Gaut, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: FICD-mediated transfer of 32P label from ATP to BiP's substrate binding domain cannot be reconciled with reported AMPylation of Thr366 or Ser365.
claims.source: In contrast, FICD-mediated transfer of 32P label from ATP to BiP's substrate binding domain, observed here in vitro, can not be reconciled with reported AMPylation of Thr366 or Ser365 (Ham et al., 2014; Sanyal et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on logical inference from the experimental data and comparison with prior reports.

claims.claim: Electrospray ionization mass spectrometry of purified recombinant BiP produced molecular masses of 71,060.1 and 71,395.6 Da for unmodified and modified BiP, respectively.
claims.source: These preparations were examined by electrospray ionization mass spectrometry and produced molecular masses of 71,060.1 and 71,395.6 Da for unmodified and modified BiP, respectively (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The mass difference of 335 Da between unmodified and modified BiP is consistent with a single covalent modification by AMP (329.12 Da).
claims.source: The mass difference of 335 Da is consistent with a single covalent modification by AMP (329.12 Da) in modified BiP.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on comparison of measured mass difference with expected mass of AMP.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry of endogenous BiP immunopurified from cycloheximide-treated wildtype CHO-K1 cells revealed only two molecular masses (70,538.3 Da and 70,866.1 Da) with a mass difference of 327.8 Da.
claims.source: An analogous mass spectrometry experiment with endogenous BiP immunopurified from cycloheximide-treated wildtype CHO-K1 cells also revealed only two molecular masses (70,538.3 Da and 70,866.1 Da) with a mass difference of 327.8 Da, consistent with modification of BiP by a single AMP moiety in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: BiP from AMPylation-deficient FICD-/- cells gave rise to a single species with a molecular mass (70,532.2 Da) similar to the predicted mass of unmodified mature BiP.
claims.source: BiP from AMPylation-deficient FICD-/- cells gave rise to a single species with a molecular mass (70,532.2 Da) that is similar to the predicted mass of unmodified mature BiP (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A unique peptide (doubly charged peak of 1374.15 m/z) corresponding in mass to an AMPylation of residues 511-532 was observed in samples digested with Arg-C.
claims.source: A unique peptide (doubly charged peak of 1374.15 m/z) corresponding in mass to an AMPylation of residues 511-532 was observed in samples digested with Arg-C
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A peptide (doubly charged peak of 916.94 m/z) corresponding to AMPylation of residues 515-528 was detected in the Asp-N digest.
claims.source: and another peptide (doubly charged peak of 916.94 m/z) corresponding to AMPylation of residues 515-528 was detected in the Asp-N digest (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: A doubly charged peak (1209.62 m/z) corresponding to the unmodified BiP 511-532 fragment was present in the Arg-C digests of unmodified BiP and absent from the spectrum of the modified form.
claims.source: Moreover, another doubly charged peak (1209.62 m/z) corresponding to the unmodified BiP 511-532 fragment was present in the Arg-C digests of unmodified BiP and absent from the spectrum of the modified form (Figure 4C, left panels)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: All four digests (chymotrypsin, trypsin, Arg-C, Asp-N) contained peptides covering Ser365 and Thr366, but these were all unmodified peptides.
claims.source: However, all four digests contained peptides covering Ser365 and Thr366, but these were all unmodified peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The specificity of FICD for AMPylation of hydroxyl side chains and the overlap of modified peptides from the two digests narrows the modification site to three residues: Thr518, Thr525 and Thr527.
claims.source: The specificity of FICD for AMPylation of hydroxyl side chains and the overlap of modified peptides from the two digests narrows the modification site to three residues: Thr518, Thr525 and Thr527.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is based on inference from the mass spectrometry data and known FICD specificity.

claims.claim: Both BiPT525A and BiPT527A remained substrates for AMPylation in vitro.
claims.source: Both BiPT525A and BiPT527A remained substrates for AMPylation in vitro, whereas the BiPT518A mutation abolished all modification of BiP (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: The BiPT518A mutation abolished all modification of BiP in vitro.
claims.source: Both BiPT525A and BiPT527A remained substrates for AMPylation in vitro, whereas the BiPT518A mutation abolished all modification of BiP (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: BiPT366A, BiPR470E, and BiPR492E were all modified by FICDE234G in vitro with varying efficiency.
claims.source: BiPT366A and BiPR470E or BiPR492E [the latter are mutations that attenuate labeling of FLAG-tagged BiP in vivo by 32P orthophosphate or 3H adenosine (Chambers et al., 2012)] were all modified by FICDE234G in vitro with varying efficiency, as was the substrate binding-deficient mutant BiPV461F (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The substrate binding-deficient mutant BiPV461F was modified by FICDE234G in vitro.
claims.source: as was the substrate binding-deficient mutant BiPV461F (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The substitution of Thr518 by either alanine or glutamic acid moderately impaired the ability of BiP to form oligomers.
claims.source: The substitution of Thr518 by either alanine or glutamic acid moderately impaired the ability of BiP to form oligomers and slightly modified the mobility of the monomeric ('A') form of BiP on native gels
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Mutating Thr366 had no effect on BiP oligomerization.
claims.source: whereas mutating Thr366 had no effect on oligomerization (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: BiPT518E could not be AMPylated in vitro.
claims.source: BiPT518E could not be AMPylated in vitro (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: BiPT518E resembled AMPylated BiP by its migration on native-PAGE and by its resistance to SubA-mediated proteolytic cleavage, whether exposed to FICDE234G or not.
claims.source: Yet, whether exposed to FICDE234G or not, BiPT518E resembled AMPylated BiP by its migration on native-PAGE and by its resistance to SubA-mediated proteolytic cleavage (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted and AMPylated BiP511-532 is reciprocally enriched in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells.
claims.source: Note that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted and AMPylated BiP511-532 is reciprocally enriched in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 6B and is supported by the SILAC data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted by cycloheximide treatment only in wildtype cells.
claims.source: Note that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted by cycloheximide treatment only in wildtype cells and AMPylated BiP511-532 is only detected in wildtype cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 6C and is supported by the SILAC data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: AMPylated BiP511-532 is only detected in wildtype cells.
claims.source: Note that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted by cycloheximide treatment only in wildtype cells and AMPylated BiP511-532 is only detected in wildtype cells.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 6C and is supported by the SILAC data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The fragmentation spectra of Arg-C peptides 511-532 from both endogenous BiP AMPylated in vivo and recombinant BiP AMPylated in vitro yielded a collection of y-ions and b-ions that included all the residues on the 511-532 peptide except Thr518.
claims.source: The fragmentation spectra of Arg-C peptides 511-532 from both endogenous BiP AMPylated in vivo, or recombinant BiP AMPylated in vitro, yielded a collection of y-ions and b-ions that included all the residues on the 511-532 peptide except Thr518, whereas the latter residue was conspicuously represented in the ion series from the fragmentation spectrum of unmodified endogenous and recombinant BiP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Thr518 was conspicuously represented in the ion series from the fragmentation spectrum of unmodified endogenous and recombinant BiP.
claims.source: whereas the latter residue was conspicuously represented in the ion series from the fragmentation spectrum of unmodified endogenous and recombinant BiP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: BiPE201G and BiPT229A exhibited enhanced AMPylation rates compared to wildtype BiP.
claims.source: BiPE201G and BiPT229A, mutants that bind ATP and undergo allosteric transitions but are defective in nucleotide hydrolysis (Gaut and Hendershot, 1993; Petrova et al., 2008; Wei et al., 1995), exhibited enhanced AMPylation rates compared to wildtype BiP (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: BiPT37G showed slightly reduced AMPylation compared to wildtype BiP.
claims.source: By contrast, BiPT37G, which is defective in ATP hydrolysis and in the allosteric transitions upon ATP binding, showed slightly reduced AMPylation
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: BiPG226D and BiPADDA remained unmodified by FICD.
claims.source: whereas mutants that are severely defective in adopting the ATP-bound conformation, such as the ATP binding-deficient BiPG226D or BiPADDA, which is locked in the domain-uncoupled state due to a four residue substitution in its interdomain linker (Laufen et al., 1999; Preissler et al., 2015), remained unmodified by FICD (Figure 7A and B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claims.claim: The isolated BiP substrate binding domain was not modified by FICDE234G.
claims.source: Consistent with an important role for the conformation of BiP in determining its ability to serve as a substrate for FICD, the isolated BiP substrate binding domain (purified from bacteria as a fusion to yeast Smt3) was not modified by FICDE234G (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The t1/2max values for in vitro AMPylation of BiPT229A (4.0 min) and BiPE201G (2.3 min) were significantly shorter than for wildtype BiP (9.9 min).
claims.source: The t1/2max values for in vitro AMPylation of BiPT229A (4.0 min) and BiPE201G (2.3 min) were significantly shorter than for wildtype BiP (9.9 min) (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: AMPylation lowered the basal ATP hydrolysis rate of BiP by ~50%.
claims.source: AMPylation lowered the basal ATP hydrolysis rate of BiP by ~50% (Figure 8A and B)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claims.claim: The ATPase activity of unmodified BiP was enhanced by the presence of a J-domain in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: and, while the ATPase activity of unmodified BiP was enhanced by the presence of a J-domain in a concentration-dependent manner, AMPylated BiP was almost entirely resistant to J-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: AMPylated BiP was almost entirely resistant to J-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis.
claims.source: and, while the ATPase activity of unmodified BiP was enhanced by the presence of a J-domain in a concentration-dependent manner, AMPylated BiP was almost entirely resistant to J-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: AMPylation barely influenced steady-state binding of substrate peptide to BiP.
claims.source: AMPylation barely influenced steady-state binding of substrate peptide to BiP: The dissociation constants of the complex between unmodified BiP or AMPylated BiP and a well-characterized substrate peptide, HTFPAVLGSC, measured at equilibrium (in the presence of ADP) by fluorescence polarization, were similar (KdBiP 16.7 µM and KdBiP-AMP 11.5 µM; Figure 8D)
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Challenge with excess of unlabeled peptide revealed a markedly higher "off" rate of the complex between AMPylated BiP and the bound peptide (koffBiP 0.037 ± 0.006 min-1 vs. koffBiP-AMP 0.212 ± 0.021 min-1).
claims.source: However, challenge with excess of unlabeled peptide revealed a markedly higher "off" rate of the complex between AMPylated BiP and the bound peptide (koffBiP 0.037 ± 0.006 min-1 vs. koffBiP-AMP 0.212 ± 0.021 min-1; Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: Enforced expression of constitutively active FICDE234G led to activation of the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
claims.source: The dormant reporter was activated by tunicamycin-induced ER stress (Figure 9A, panels 1 and 2; a positive control), and by acquisition of a constitutively active FICDE234G but not by a catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A nor by the regulated wildtype enzyme (Figure 9A, panels 3-5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A did not activate the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
claims.source: and by acquisition of a constitutively active FICDE234G but not by a catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A nor by the regulated wildtype enzyme (Figure 9A, panels 3-5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The regulated wildtype FICD enzyme did not activate the CHOP::GFP UPR reporter.
claims.source: and by acquisition of a constitutively active FICDE234G but not by a catalytically dead FICDE234G-H363A nor by the regulated wildtype enzyme (Figure 9A, panels 3-5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: The induction of the UPR reporter in CHO-K1 cells was mirrored by the behavior of endogenous BiP, whose levels increased in a time-dependent manner in human HEK 293 cells upon activation of a conditional allele encoding FICDE234G.
claims.source: The induction of the UPR reporter in CHO-K1 cells was mirrored by the behavior of endogenous BiP, whose levels increased in a time-dependent manner in human HEK 293 cells upon activation of a conditional allele encoding FICDE234G (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Sustained FICDE234G expression had an adverse effect on cell viability.
claims.source: As suggested previously (Sanyal et al., 2015), the capacity of the cells to compensate for the consequences of deregulated FICD activity is limited; reflected here by the adverse effect of sustained FICDE234G expression on cell viability (Figure 9D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: FICD knockout led to a conspicuous temporal delay in PERK and IRE1α autophosphorylation in AR42j cells exposed to DTT.
claims.source: FICD knockout led to a conspicuous temporal delay in PERK and IRE1α autophosphorylation, observed in two independently derived AR42j FICD-/- clones (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and is supported by data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: Pre-exposure to cycloheximide attenuated subsequent translational repression by DTT-mediated PERK activation in FICD-/- cells.
claims.source: In this experiment, wildtype or FICD-/- AR42j cells were pre-exposed to cycloheximide for 3 hr followed by brief washout to allow recovery of protein synthesis, which was measured by incorporation of puromycin label into newly synthesized proteins. In wildtype cells, DTT led to marked attenuation of protein synthesis, regardless of pre-exposure to cycloheximide (Figure 10E, compare lanes 1 and 2 and 3 and 4), however pre-exposure to cycloheximide attenuated subsequent translational repression by DTT-mediated PERK activation in FICD-/- cells (Figure 10E, lanes 5-8).

results.result: FICD is necessary and sufficient for BiP modification in mammalian cells. Deletion of FICD abolished detectable modification of endogenous BiP (C1, C28, C29), while enforced overexpression of constitutively active FICDE234G restored the acidic form of BiP in FICD-/- cells (C32). Wildtype FICD did not promote BiP's acidic form even when strongly overexpressed (C33).
results.evaluation: Multiple independent lines of evidence converge: CRISPR-mediated FICD knockout eliminates the 'B' form on native-PAGE (C28), the acidic form on IEF-PAGE (C29), and SubA resistance (C28). Rescue experiments with constitutively active FICDE234G restore modification (C32), while wildtype FICD does not (C33), demonstrating both necessity and sufficiency with appropriate controls.

results.result: FICD AMPylates BiP on a single residue, Thr518, both in vitro and in vivo. Mass spectrometry of intact BiP showed a mass difference consistent with single AMP addition (C48-C51). Peptide mapping identified modified peptides spanning residues 511-532 (C52-C54), and mutagenesis narrowed the site to Thr518 (C56-C58).
results.evaluation: The identification of Thr518 as the AMPylation site is supported by multiple complementary approaches: intact protein mass spectrometry showing single modification (C48-C51), peptide mapping by multiple proteases (C52-C54), and definitive mutagenesis showing BiPT518A abolishes modification while BiPT525A and BiPT527A remain substrates (C57-C58). The convergence of these independent methods provides strong support.

results.result: SILAC-based mass spectrometry confirmed Thr518 as the AMPylation site in vivo. Unmodified BiP511-532 was depleted and AMPylated BiP511-532 was enriched in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells (C65-C67). Fragmentation spectra of AMPylated peptides lacked ions spanning Thr518, while unmodified peptides contained them (C68-C69).
results.evaluation: The SILAC approach provides quantitative evidence for FICD-dependent and cycloheximide-responsive AMPylation at Thr518 in vivo (C65-C67). The fragmentation pattern analysis (C68-C69) provides site-specific confirmation. The use of FICD-/- cells as a negative control strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: BiP AMPylation increases when protein flux into the ER is attenuated and decreases during ER stress. Cycloheximide treatment increased the 'B' form and SubA resistance (C5, C24-C26), while ER stress with 2-deoxyglucose decreased them (C34-C35). Recovery from stress restored modification (C36).
results.evaluation: The inverse correlation between unfolded protein burden and BiP modification is demonstrated through multiple experimental manipulations (cycloheximide, 2-deoxyglucose, washout) with consistent results across different assays (native-PAGE, SubA resistance, IEF-PAGE). The observation that FICD mRNA increases during stress while modification decreases (C35) suggests post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: BiP in the ATP-bound conformation is the preferred substrate for FICD. ATP hydrolysis-deficient mutants (BiPE201G, BiPT229A) showed enhanced AMPylation rates (C70, C74), while mutants defective in adopting the ATP-bound conformation (BiPG226D, BiPADDA) were not modified (C72). The isolated substrate binding domain was not modified (C73).
results.evaluation: The conformational dependence of AMPylation is demonstrated through systematic analysis of well-characterized BiP mutants with defined conformational properties (C70-C72). The kinetic measurements (C74) provide quantitative support. The requirement for the full-length protein (C73) and the structural analysis of Thr518 accessibility in different conformational states provide mechanistic insight.

results.result: AMPylation reduces BiP's basal ATPase activity by ~50% and abolishes J-protein-mediated stimulation of ATP hydrolysis. AMPylated BiP showed reduced basal ATP hydrolysis (C75) and was almost entirely resistant to J-domain stimulation (C77), while unmodified BiP responded normally (C76).
results.evaluation: The functional consequences of AMPylation on BiP's ATPase activity are demonstrated through direct biochemical measurements with purified components (C75-C77). The use of completely AMPylated BiP and appropriate controls (unmodified BiP, mutant J-domain) strengthens the conclusions. Statistical analysis confirms significance (C75).

results.result: AMPylation increases the peptide dissociation rate from BiP 6-fold without substantially affecting steady-state binding affinity. Equilibrium dissociation constants were similar for modified and unmodified BiP (C78), but the off-rate was markedly higher for AMPylated BiP (C79, C6).
results.evaluation: The substrate binding analysis using fluorescence polarization provides quantitative kinetic data (C78-C79). The 6-fold increase in off-rate (C6, C79) with minimal change in equilibrium binding (C78) indicates that AMPylation affects the kinetics rather than thermodynamics of substrate binding, consistent with an ATP-like state.

results.result: Deregulated FICD activity activates the UPR and reduces cell viability. Constitutively active FICDE234G activated the CHOP::GFP reporter (C80) and increased BiP levels (C83), while catalytically dead or wildtype FICD did not (C81-C82). Sustained FICDE234G expression reduced cell viability (C84).
results.evaluation: The UPR activation by constitutively active FICD is demonstrated through multiple readouts (reporter activation C80, endogenous BiP induction C83, cell viability C84) with appropriate negative controls (catalytically dead and wildtype FICD, C81-C82). The observations are consistent across different cell lines and support the inactivating nature of AMPylation.

results.result: FICD deletion enhances ER buffering capacity under specific conditions. FICD knockout delayed PERK and IRE1α autophosphorylation in cycloheximide-pretreated cells exposed to DTT (C85-C86), but had no effect on tunicamycin-induced UPR activation (C87).
results.evaluation: The enhanced buffering capacity in FICD-/- cells is demonstrated in two independent clones (C85) with multiple UPR readouts (PERK/IRE1α phosphorylation, protein synthesis). The context-dependence (requiring cycloheximide pretreatment, C86-C87) is important and well-documented. However, the transient nature and specific conditions required suggest this may be a subtle phenotype.

results.result: FICD reconstitutes BiP modification in vitro with properties matching endogenous modification. Active FICDE234G produced a 'B' form resistant to SubA cleavage (C37-C38), with an acidic pI (C39-C40), and efficiently transferred 32P from ATP to BiP (C43). Modification went to completion yielding a single acidic form (C40-C42).
results.evaluation: The in vitro reconstitution experiments demonstrate that FICD is sufficient to produce all the characteristic features of modified BiP observed in cells (native-PAGE mobility, SubA resistance, acidic pI, radiolabeling). The use of multiple FICD preparations (bacterial and mammalian) and the observation of complete, homogeneous modification (C40-C42) strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: FICD-mediated radiolabeling maps to BiP's substrate binding domain, consistent with historical metabolic labeling but inconsistent with reported Thr366/Ser365 modification. SubA cleavage of radiolabeled BiP showed label only in the SBD fragment (C44-C45), matching prior CnBr mapping (C46) but contradicting reported NBD modification sites (C47).
results.evaluation: The domain mapping using SubA cleavage and radiolabeling (C44-C45) provides clear evidence for SBD modification. The consistency with historical CnBr mapping (C46) and inconsistency with reported Thr366/Ser365 sites (C47) is explicitly noted. This result is important for reconciling conflicting prior reports.

results.result: Ser365 and Thr366 are not modified by FICD under the conditions tested. All four protease digests contained unmodified peptides covering Ser365/Thr366 (C55), and BiPT366A was modified by FICD in vitro (C59).
results.evaluation: The evidence against Ser365/Thr366 modification is strong: multiple protease digests all show unmodified peptides at these sites (C55) in samples where BiP is completely modified (as shown by IEF-PAGE and intact mass). The ability of BiPT366A to be modified (C59) provides additional support. This directly contradicts prior reports.

results.result: The T518E mutation mimics some effects of AMPylation. BiPT518E could not be AMPylated (C63) but resembled AMPylated BiP in native-PAGE migration and SubA resistance (C64). Thr518 mutations moderately impaired oligomerization while Thr366 mutation had no effect (C61-C62).
results.evaluation: The phosphomimetic analysis provides insight into the structural consequences of modification at Thr518. The observation that T518E mimics AMPylation in some assays (C64) but cannot be AMPylated (C63) is internally consistent. The differential effects of Thr518 vs Thr366 mutations on oligomerization (C61-C62) support the functional importance of Thr518.

results.result: Cycloheximide treatment produces a high-mobility 'B' form of BiP that is resistant to SubA cleavage. This form accumulates upon protein synthesis inhibition (C24) and is consumed during calcium depletion to form oligomers (C25). The 'B' form shares SubA resistance with the acidic modified form (C26-C27).
results.evaluation: The characterization of the 'B' form on native-PAGE provides a convenient assay for BiP modification. The correlation with SubA resistance (C26-C27) and the dynamic behavior in response to cycloheximide and calcium depletion (C24-C25) are well-documented. This establishes the 'B' form as a proxy for modified BiP.

results.result: FICD activity is regulated by autoinhibition. The E234G mutation de-represses FICD (C30), while the H363A mutation abolishes AMPylation activity (C31).
results.evaluation: These claims describe established properties of FICD mutants based on prior work (citations provided). The observations are used throughout the manuscript to manipulate FICD activity experimentally. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: FICD-mediated AMPylation on Thr518 is the major detectable covalent modification of BiP and accounts for its key features. The findings unify prior observations regarding BiP modification (C88) and explain its acidity and inertness (C89).
results.evaluation: These integrative claims in the Discussion are well-supported by the totality of experimental evidence. The elimination of all detectable modification in FICD-/- cells (C1, C28-C29), the single modification site identified by mass spectrometry (C48-C58), and the functional consequences (C75-C79) collectively support these conclusions.

results.result: Structural analysis suggests that ATP binding enhances Thr518 accessibility to FICD. Thr518 is highly conserved (C90), and mobilization of the Thr518 side chain by ATP binding is suggested to enhance solvent exposure (C91).
results.evaluation: The structural interpretation is based on published crystal structures (PDB 5E86, 5E84) showing loss of stabilizing interactions in the ATP state. This provides a mechanistic explanation for the conformational dependence of AMPylation (C70-C74, C92). The conservation of Thr518 (C90) supports functional importance.

results.result: Prior work established that BiP undergoes activity-dependent post-translational modification and is subject to multiple regulatory mechanisms. These claims summarize established knowledge and prior reports about BiP function, modification, and regulation.
results.evaluation: These claims accurately represent prior work as evidenced by appropriate citations. They provide essential context for the current study. The authors note conflicting reports about AMPylation (C22-C23), which their work aims to resolve.

results.result: FICD deletion abolishes detectable modification of endogenous BiP in mammalian cells, as evidenced by the absence of the SubA-resistant 'B' form and the acidic form of BiP in FICD-/- cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that the authors 'convincingly demonstrate' that 'FICD modifies a single site in the substrate binding domain of BiP both in vitro and in cells.' The reviewers acknowledge the manuscript as 'solid and interesting' and note no concerns about the FICD knockout data showing loss of BiP modification.

results.result: FICD AMPylates BiP on a single residue, Thr518, as determined by mass spectrometry and mutagenesis experiments both in vitro and in vivo.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state the authors 'convincingly demonstrate' that 'the primary modification site is T518.' However, reviewers raise concerns about potential heterogeneity in the BiP-AMP sample (Essential revision 3 and 5), requesting analysis of tailing LC peaks and clarification of biphasic dissociation kinetics, suggesting some uncertainty about sample homogeneity.

results.result: The modification site is in the substrate binding domain, not at previously reported sites Thr366 or Ser365 in the nucleotide binding domain.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this finding as part of the manuscript's contribution to resolving contradictory prior reports. Essential revision 1 requests discussion of how modification at T518 can account for previous findings, indicating acceptance of the new site identification but requesting reconciliation with prior literature.

results.result: AMPylation of BiP reduces its basal ATP hydrolysis rate by ~50% and abolishes stimulation of ATP hydrolysis by J-domain cofactors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the claim that 'AMPylation of BiP reduces BiPs ATPase rate and renders it less-responsive to J domain containing proteins' but express surprise in Essential revision 6, stating 'Failure of a J domain to stimulate hydrolysis of the modified protein is somewhat surprising' and request additional experiments to determine if the J domain still binds BiP-AMP.

results.result: AMPylation enhances peptide dissociation from BiP 6-fold while barely influencing steady-state peptide binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note in Essential revision 5 that 'The kinetics of peptide dissociation from BiP-AMP looks very biphasic' and request biphasic fitting and error bars. They state 'Figure 8E is the best evidence that AMPylation of BiP has an effect on the behavior of the chaperone in vitro, so the data need to be convincing,' indicating the data require strengthening.

results.result: FICD deletion enhances ER buffering capacity and causes a temporal delay in UPR activation under specific conditions (cycloheximide pre-treatment), but has no effect on UPR kinetics during direct ER stress (tunicamycin).
results.evaluation: Reviewers note 'One weakness of the paper is that the effects of constitutive AMPylation or inhibited AMPylation on UPR signaling are relatively small' and state 'The subtle change in the kinetics of UPR activation that was observed in the FIDC null cells is probably not sufficient to warrant the title of the manuscript.' This indicates the physiological significance remains unclear.

results.result: Deregulated FICD activity (constitutively active FICDE234G) activates the UPR, increases BiP levels, and has adverse effects on cell viability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that the authors demonstrate 'excessive AMPylation of BiP is toxic to cells due to constitutive activation of the UPR.' However, Essential revision 4 requests clarification of discrepancies in the FL/BiP ratio data in the absence of doxycycline, suggesting minor concerns about data interpretation.

results.result: AMPylation increases in a FICD-dependent manner when protein flux into the ER is attenuated (cycloheximide treatment) and decreases during ER stress (2-deoxyglucose), despite increased FICD mRNA levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about these findings. Essential revision 2 asks whether FICD is induced by the UPR and how this fits the authors' hypothesis, indicating acceptance of the data but requesting broader contextualization.

results.result: BiP in the ATP-bound conformation is the preferred substrate for FICD, as demonstrated by enhanced AMPylation of hydrolysis-deficient mutants and lack of modification of domain-uncoupled mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these findings. Essential revision 1 requests discussion of 'how a modification of a threonine residue in a loop linking the SBD and how NBD could affect ATP hydrolysis,' indicating acceptance of the conformational preference data but requesting mechanistic explanation.

results.result: In vitro reconstitution experiments demonstrate that FICD can modify recombinant BiP to produce the 'B' form with properties matching endogenous modified BiP, including SubA resistance and acidic pI.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the in vitro reconstitution data. These findings support the identification of FICD as the enzyme responsible for BiP modification and are part of the 'convincing' demonstration acknowledged by reviewers.

results.result: Cycloheximide treatment leads to accumulation of a high mobility 'B' form of BiP that is resistant to SubA cleavage, while calcium depletion draws on this pool to promote BiP oligomer assembly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these characterization experiments. These findings establish the biochemical properties of modified BiP that are later connected to FICD activity.

results.result: The constitutively active FICDE234G mutant, but not wildtype FICD or catalytically dead FICDH363A, promotes the acidic form of BiP when overexpressed.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about these mutant characterization experiments. These findings establish the tools used throughout the study and demonstrate the regulated nature of FICD activity.

results.result: Mutation of Thr518 to alanine or glutamic acid affects BiP oligomerization, and the T518E mutant mimics AMPylated BiP in its biochemical properties without being a substrate for FICD.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about these mutagenesis experiments. These findings support the functional importance of Thr518 and provide a phosphomimetic tool for studying AMPylation effects.

results.result: FICD-mediated AMPylation on Thr518 is the major, if not the only, covalent modification of BiP detectable by existing methods and is sufficient to account for previously observed features of modified BiP.
results.evaluation: Essential revision 1 requests 'a serious discussion of the previous data reported by the Ron group and other labs to clarify whether a modification at T518 can account for the previous findings,' and Essential revision 3 questions whether the conclusion of 'modification of a single site (T518) can account for all previous evidence' is fully supported given potential heterogeneity in mass spectrometry samples.

results.result: SILAC mass spectrometry demonstrates that unmodified BiP511-532 is depleted and AMPylated BiP511-532 is enriched in cycloheximide-treated wildtype cells, with this modification being FICD-dependent.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the SILAC data. These experiments provide orthogonal evidence for FICD-dependent modification of the identified peptide region in cells.

comparisons.comparison: Both agree that FICD knockout eliminates BiP modification (C1, C28, C29). OpenEval emphasizes the multiple independent lines of evidence including rescue experiments (C32, C33), while peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'convincingly demonstrate' FICD's role. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED.

Both address Thr518 identification as the AMPylation site (C4, C48-C58). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED through convergence of mass spectrometry, peptide mapping, and mutagenesis. Peer reviewers also state the authors 'convincingly demonstrate' T518 is the primary site but raise concerns about potential sample heterogeneity (Essential revisions 3, 5), marking it SUPPORTED with caveats.

Both address SILAC evidence for in vivo AMPylation (C65-C67). OpenEval finds the quantitative SILAC approach and fragmentation analysis (C68-C69) SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the SILAC data, marking it SUPPORTED as orthogonal evidence for FICD-dependent modification.

Both address the inverse correlation between unfolded protein burden and BiP modification (C5, C34-C36). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED through multiple experimental manipulations. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED without specific concerns, though Essential revision 2 requests broader contextualization regarding FICD induction.

Both address conformational dependence of AMPylation (C70-C74, C92). OpenEval finds the systematic analysis of BiP mutants and kinetic measurements SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, requesting mechanistic explanation in Essential revision 1 but not questioning the data itself.

Both address effects of AMPylation on BiP's ATPase activity (C75-C77). OpenEval finds the direct biochemical measurements SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, expressing surprise that J domain fails to stimulate hydrolysis and requesting additional experiments to determine if J domain still binds BiP-AMP.

Both address substrate binding kinetics (C6, C78-C79). OpenEval finds the fluorescence polarization data SUPPORTED, showing 6-fold increase in off-rate. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, noting biphasic kinetics in Figure 8E and requesting biphasic fitting and error bars, stating 'the data need to be convincing.'

Both address UPR activation by constitutively active FICD (C2, C80-C84). OpenEval finds the multiple readouts SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers acknowledge the demonstration but mark it SUPPORTED with minor concerns about FL/BiP ratio discrepancies (Essential revision 4).

Both address enhanced buffering capacity in FICD-/- cells (C2, C85-C87). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED but notes the phenotype is subtle and context-dependent. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, stating 'One weakness of the paper is that the effects...are relatively small' and 'The subtle change...is probably not sufficient to warrant the title.'

Both address in vitro reconstitution experiments (C37-C46). OpenEval finds the demonstration that FICD is sufficient to produce all characteristic features of modified BiP SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED without specific concerns, as part of the 'convincing' demonstration.

OpenEval addresses domain mapping (C44-C47) showing SBD modification and inconsistency with Thr366/Ser365. Peer R10 addresses broader in vitro reconstitution (C37-C46) including some domain mapping claims. Both find evidence SUPPORTED. Peer R3 specifically addresses evidence against Ser365/Thr366 (C47, C55, C59).

Both address evidence against Ser365/Thr366 modification (C47, C55, C59). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED through multiple protease digests and mutagenesis. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED, acknowledging the contribution to resolving contradictory reports, though Essential revision 1 requests reconciliation with prior literature.

Both address phosphomimetic analysis at Thr518 (C61-C64). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED, noting T518E mimics AMPylation in some assays but cannot be AMPylated. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED without specific concerns about these mutagenesis experiments.

Both address characterization of the 'B' form on native-PAGE (C24-C27). OpenEval finds the correlation with SubA resistance and dynamic behavior SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers also find it SUPPORTED without specific concerns, establishing the 'B' form as a proxy for modified BiP.

Both address established properties of FICD mutants (C30-C33). OpenEval finds these claims SUPPORTED based on cited literature. Peer reviewers also find them SUPPORTED without concerns, as these establish tools used throughout the study.

Both address integrative conclusions about FICD as sole enzyme and T518 as sole site (C88-C89). OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by totality of evidence. Peer reviewers mark it UNCERTAIN, requesting discussion of how T518 modification accounts for previous findings and questioning whether the conclusion is fully supported given potential sample heterogeneity.

OpenEval addresses structural interpretation of Thr518 accessibility (C90-C92) finding it SUPPORTED based on crystal structures. Peer R9 addresses conformational dependence experiments (C70-C74, C91-C92) finding them SUPPORTED. Both agree on the conformational aspects, with peer reviewers requesting mechanistic explanation.
